## Two Revolutions {.contact-slide}

<div class="two-fields">
  <div class="field-block ai-block">AI</div>
  <div class="meeting-core">health<br>biology</div>
  <div class="field-block quantum-block">Quantum</div>
</div>

<div class="slide-line">
AI is changing science now.<br>
Quantum may change what comes next.
</div>

::: {.notes}
AI is already changing the scientific landscape and the way research is done.

Quantum computing is not yet at the same practical stage, but a possible quantum
revolution is visible.

The interesting opportunity is not to put AI and quantum in opposition. It is to
ask how the two fields can exchange ideas, tools, questions, and benchmarks.
:::

## Why Benchmarks {.benchmark-slide}

<div class="benchmark-graphic">
  <div class="method method-a">AI</div>
  <div class="method method-b">Hybrid</div>
  <div class="method method-c">Quantum</div>
  <div class="benchmark-core">common<br>benchmark</div>
  <div class="evidence-pill">comparable evidence</div>
</div>

<div class="slide-line">
Claims need comparison.<br>
Comparison needs benchmarks.
</div>

::: {.notes}
Optimization is one of the main possible application areas for quantum computing,
even if it is not the only one.

Sampling, inference, simulation, reconstruction and learning may also matter when
they are connected to real scientific questions and can be made benchmarkable.

The central point is this: without shared benchmarks, progress is difficult to
compare. Strong claims need common reference problems, common metrics, and strong
classical, AI, hybrid and quantum baselines.
:::

## Two Paths {.paths-slide}

<div class="paths-grid">
  <div class="path-panel controlled">Controlled</div>
  <div class="plus-sign">+</div>
  <div class="path-panel real">Health &amp; bio</div>
</div>

<div class="path-caption">A portfolio, not one problem.</div>

::: {.notes}
We see two complementary directions.

The first is controlled theoretical problems: clean enough to measure performance,
but with many contact points with real optimization difficulty. These are heavily
used in the literature, but the field still lacks a systematic shared repository.

The second direction is health and biology. These problems are messier, but they
are scientifically meaningful: genomics, imaging, mechanistic biology, clinical
decisions, operational optimization.

The inspiration is close to Daniel Egger's decathlon idea: not a single benchmark
that pretends to represent everything, but a portfolio of different challenges.
:::

## What We Do Here {.workflow-slide}

<div class="timeline">
  <div class="timeline-step">Talks</div>
  <div class="timeline-step">Tables</div>
  <div class="timeline-step">Outputs</div>
</div>

<div class="roundtable-band">5 round tables &middot; human discussion &middot; AI-assisted notes</div>

<div class="slide-line">
Talks today.<br>
Round tables tomorrow.<br>
Shared benchmarks after.
</div>

::: {.notes}
The talks today are not only presentations. They are input for tomorrow.

Tomorrow the workshop becomes a working session: five round tables, prepared themes,
JRC facilitators and note takers, and invited experts from different fields.

We also want to experiment with the way the workshop works. The main value remains
the in-person discussion, but AI-assisted tools such as Kiro can help capture,
structure and improve the working documents when useful.

The expected output is concrete: candidate benchmark problems, datasets, metrics,
baselines, repository structure, and a possible paper, report, roadmap or policy note.

The bigger reason is that common benchmarks can improve research comparability and
collaboration, and can also help public institutions think about infrastructure,
investment and future policy direction.
:::
